rewrite:
A bought lead list makes you send 1,000 emails to reach the 20 people who happen to be ready. You burn the other 980 to get there.

The data is fine the day you buy it. It goes stale right after, and you keep working it like it's still live. A list is a name, a title, a company, and a timestamp from whenever someone scraped it. It tells you who a person was, and nothing about what's happening in their market this week.

And this week is what matters. Someone who looked perfect six months ago might have just signed with your competitor. Someone who ghosted you last quarter might have raised a round on Tuesday and is buying everything in sight.

Here's how to build from the motion instead of the list:

1. Pick the moments that come right before a purchase. Someone opens a role they only open right before they buy. Someone drops the tool you replace. Someone closes a round.

2. Watch for those moments. Demand never sits still, and companies start looking for a vendor well before they land on anyone's radar.

3. Score the why-now on every account that moves.

4. Pick the handful that matter and let the rest be. This is where most of the work is: restraint.

5. Only then send an email, written off the real trigger.

TL;DR: A bought lead list tells you who people were. The market tells you who is ready now. Build from the second one.

rewrite:
Not every buying signal deserves a human. Here's a routing rule to decide who responds to each one.

Score each account by readiness, then send it to one of four responders:

1. Human, today. The pricing page hit repeatedly this week, a competitor or review-site comparison, or an inbound reply. High intent and time-sensitive. A person sends a short, specific note.

2. Agent. A role opened that maps to a pain you solve, or a tech or integration change. Real but early. An agent runs a value-first touch, no pitch.

3. Nurture. A single download or a newsletter open. Curiosity, without intent yet. It goes on an educational drip until something stronger shows up.

4. Ignore. No fit, or every signal is stale. Suppress it so it stops eating attention.

Two rules keep it honest. When signals conflict, route to the higher tier and say why. And never act on a signal that isn't actually there.

Without a rule, a content download and a week of pricing-page visits land in the same queue, and the hot accounts go cold while someone writes a careful note to a tire-kicker.

The prompt to run this rubric is in the reply below.

rewrite:
How to find the signal pairs worth acting on, using your own closed deals:

1. Take your last ten closed deals.
2. Go back thirty days before the first real conversation at each account.
3. Write down everything that was happening there.
4. Mark the signals that showed up together.
5. For each pair, ask: do these two answer different questions, or the same question louder?

Step 5 is the one that matters. Two signals at the same account beat any single signal, but only when they are different kinds.

Say someone at a target account starts engaging your competitor's posts. On its own, mild. Then a role opens on that team to own the exact problem you solve. Also mild. Together, one says they are shopping and the other says somebody is now accountable for fixing it. Two different questions, both answered in the same month.

Two social signals work differently. One person likes a post, someone else comments a week later. It feels like momentum, and it is the same fact twice. Most setups reward this kind, because social fires constantly and a pair is easy to find.

Keep the pairs that answer different questions, and watch for those combinations going forward.

Build your AI outbound stack in this order. If reply rates are flat, check whether you started at the wrong end.

1. Signals first.
Pick four triggers and wire them in before you touch anything else. Options: reposted jobs, fundraising rounds, M&A filings, tenders and RFPs, competitor engagement. Each one marks a different buying moment.

2. Scoring next.
ICP fit x signal recency x buying-stage weight. A job reposted in the last seven days at an ICP-fit account beats a job posting from six weeks ago at a non-ICP account. Decide who you act on this week, and who falls into next month.

3. Message context last.
Pass the exact role being reposted, the exact funding amount, the exact tender description into whatever writes the first line. Generic "fits your ICP" filler tells the model nothing useful.

Each layer feeds the next: the signal triggers scoring, scoring filters who matters this week, context shapes the message.

Run this loop.
